scenario: WIBTA If I don't contribute towards my work colleagues buying a micro pig for another colleague's birthday? | Tldr: my colleagues bought me fish which I wasn't expecting in the past for my birthday. Another colleague's birthday is coming up and they want to buy them a pig and I don't really agree. WIBTA if I don't contribute? I really wish this was a joke but let me explain. This colleague of mine is about to turn 40. We will call them George if that's okay. Nothing against her she is a great person. Now George still lives at home with their parents and owns a dog. They are going through the phase of desperately dating around, and they have always wanted a micro pig. My colleagues love to celebrate birthdays. They bought me fish, bless them, for my 20th birthday because I was very lonely at the time as I had just moved out from my parents house etc. I really appreciated the thought and I love my fish dearly, but sometimes I feel a little bit tied down by them, as I'm not always at home (I spend a lot of time around my boyfriend 's house) and one day I eventually want to move away and that may be an issue with fish as if be looking to go to another house share. Don't get me wrong I really really appreciated the thought, but I don't think they took into consideration the commitment it takes to look after an animal. They did mean we'll though. Although I expressed slight interest in what I would hypothetically name an axolotl before my birthday, I never ever expected to see fish when I walked into my room. I am currently in a house share with a colleague, as it was the only viable option at the time. Back to George, my concern is they still live at home and it really isn't fair on their parents to bring a surprise pig into the house. I'm also concerned about how the pig will interact with the dog. If course I want to celebrate their birthday, but I just simply don't agree with buying someone a micro pig without taking into consideration the commitments that go into looking after them. Besides little guppies are very different to a micro pig. So will I be the asshole if I just buy my own gift for them?

Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

prediction.raw: This is a nuanced situation with ethical, practical, and emotional layers. Here’s my breakdown of whether you’d be the "asshole" (WIBTA) or not, along with the reasoning: --- ### **Score: 0 (Not the asshole)** **Why?** 1. **You’re Not Obligated to Contribute to a Gift You Disagree With** - The fact that your colleagues bought you fish (even if well-intentioned) doesn’t create a precedent for you to feel pressured to contribute to *any* gift, especially one you fundamentally disagree with. Their past gesture was a one-time thing tied to a specific circumstance (your loneliness), not a rule for future gifts. You’re not obligated to reciprocate in kind or at all. 2. **Your Concerns Are Valid and Ethical** - Your objections are reasonable: - **Lifestyle mismatch**: George’s living situation (with parents) and their current phase of "desperately dating around" suggest they may not be in a stable environment to care for a pig long-term. This could become a burden for their parents or George themselves. - **Animal welfare**: Micro pigs are not low-maintenance pets. They require space, training, diet, and socialization (especially with a dog, which could lead to stress or conflict). Your colleagues seem to have overlooked these realities. - **Surprise gifts**: You mentioned being surprised by the fish, which implies this is a pattern of "surprise" gifts that might not align with the recipient’s actual needs or preferences. George might not even *want* a pig—they might just be along for the ride in this group dynamic. 3. **You’re Not the Gatekeeper of Their Birthday** - Their intention is to celebrate George’s birthday, not to force a pig on them. If George *actually* wants a pig and is prepared for the commitment, they’ll likely appreciate the gift regardless of your contribution. If they don’t, they’ll probably feel conflicted or resentful if the group pushes it on them. - Your role is to celebrate George, not to police the group’s gift choices. You can contribute to their birthday in other ways (e.g., a card, a small personal gift, or even just showing up with a bottle of wine) without endorsing the pig. 4. **You’re Not the Asshole for Prioritizing Your Own Boundaries** - You’ve already expressed that the fish were a surprise you didn’t expect, and you’re now dealing with the practical realities of pet ownership. That’s completely valid. You’re not being unreasonable for wanting to avoid being tied down by a pet you can’t commit to long-term (especially since you’re in a house share and may move again). - Your feelings about the fish are understandable—surprise gifts can be overwhelming, especially when they’re tied to emotional circumstances (like your loneliness). This doesn’t mean you’re ungrateful; it means you have boundaries. 5. **The Group Dynamic Isn’t Your Responsibility to Fix** - If your colleagues are insistent on buying a pig, that’s their choice. You don’t have to join in if it doesn’t align with your values or circumstances. You can: - Politely decline to contribute to the pig fund and explain why (e.g., "I love celebrating George’s birthday, but I don’t think a pig is the right fit for their current situation"). - Contribute to a separate, smaller gift for George (e.g., a nice dinner out, a book, or a gift card to a spa). - Suggest alternatives that the group might consider (e.g., a donation to an animal shelter in George’s name, a fun experience like a cooking class, or a gift card to a pet store for *George* to choose their own pet if they’re serious). 6. **You’re Not the Only Voice** - If others in the group share your concerns, they can also voice them. But you don’t have to wait for them—your perspective matters, and it’s okay to speak up for what you believe is right. --- ### **What You *Could* Do Instead:** - **Contribute to a smaller, more practical gift** for George (e.g., a gift card to their favorite restaurant, a cozy blanket, or a subscription to a service they’d enjoy). - **Host a birthday activity** (e.g., organize a game night, a movie marathon, or a potluck) where the focus is on spending time with George rather than buying a pet. - **Buy a gift for yourself** (e.g., a nice dinner out with your boyfriend) and use the money you’d have spent on the pig to treat yourself. This sends a clear message that you’re not obligated to participate in this gift. - **Have an honest conversation with George** (privately) about your concerns. For example: > *"I just wanted to check in—this group gift is really sweet, but I’m worried about the practicalities of a pig for you right now. If you’re serious about getting one, I’d love to help you figure out the best way to do it responsibly. Otherwise, I’d be happy to contribute to something else!"* This gives George agency to decide what they want and shows you’re thinking of their best interests. --- ### **Why This Isn’t About Being "The Asshole":** - You’re not refusing to celebrate George’s birthday. You’re refusing to endorse a gift that could cause harm or inconvenience. - You’re not being selfish—you’re being thoughtful about the long-term impact of the gift. - You’re not trying to control the group’s choices. You’re simply declining to participate in something that doesn’t align with your values or circumstances. --- ### **Potential Pitfalls to Avoid:** - **Ghosting the group**: If you decline to contribute to the pig, it’s fine to still show up to celebrate George. Just explain your stance politely. - **Over-apologizing**: You don’t owe anyone an explanation, but if someone asks why you’re not contributing, a simple *"I don’t think a pig is the right fit for George right now"* is sufficient. - **Assuming George wants the pig**: Don’t project your assumptions onto George. They might genuinely want a pig, and if so, they’ll appreciate the gesture regardless of your contribution. --- ### **Final Thought:** Your colleagues’ past gift to you doesn’t create a debt that you must repay in kind. You’re allowed to have boundaries, especially when those boundaries are rooted in ethical concerns or practical realities. By declining to contribute to the pig, you’re not being the asshole—you’re being a considerate and responsible person who prioritizes what’s best for George and for yourself. **TL;DR:** You’re not the asshole. Your concerns are valid, and you’re not obligated to participate in a gift you disagree with. Celebrate George in a way that feels right for you!
